migrationNotes: Spine: follow the carbon. A sapling gains 75 kg while the soil loses almost nothing, so the atoms must come from the air; the equation names the process, counting carbon fixes how many molecules it takes, and a short look at energy and at what limits the rate closes the loop.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-light-to-sugar-hook, -5, -carbon-why. Plants respiring is taught in the next lesson, where respiration is introduced, so -5 is not asked here.

lesson.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lead.text: Start with what the tree is made of. Wood, leaves and roots are built mostly from carbon-based molecules such as sugars and the long chains made from them, and those molecules also contain hydrogen and oxygen. So the tree's extra 75 kg is mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms that were not in the tree before.

The soil cannot be their main source, because it lost only 60 grams while the tree gained 75 kilograms, over a thousand times as much. The rainwater supplies hydrogen and oxygen. Carbon is the harder one, because water holds almost none. The only large store of carbon within reach of a leaf is the air, where it travels as carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out. A leaf takes carbon dioxide in through tiny pores and builds its carbon into sugar.
Light does not supply atoms. Sunshine is energy, and energy is not made of matter. It plays a different part, which comes a few screens later.
Rainwater carries almost no carbon, and light carries none at all.

steps.headline: Building sugar from air and water

lead.text: A leaf does this job in its cells, in the chloroplasts you met in the first lesson. The process is called photosynthesis, which means putting together with light. The leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from its roots, and uses light energy to join them into a sugar called glucose. Oxygen is left over, and the leaf releases it to the air.

Chemists write this as an equation. Each formula stands for one molecule, and the number in front says how many molecules take part: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Read it as six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules, with light, making one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules. The small numbers inside a formula count atoms, so C₆H₁₂O₆ is a molecule built from 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms.

afterFigure.text: Glucose is the sugar the leaf makes first, and the rest of its chemistry starts from it. The figure shows the equation for one glucose and for two, and the next screens count atoms through it.

lead.text: The number written in front of a formula counts molecules.

The equation also lets you follow the atoms. Atoms are rearranged in a reaction and are never created or destroyed, so every carbon atom in the glucose must have come from a carbon atom that went in. The only carbon on the left of the equation is in carbon dioxide, and each CO₂ molecule holds exactly one carbon atom.
A glucose molecule holds six carbon atoms, so it takes six CO₂ molecules to supply them. Make five glucose molecules and the leaf needs 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, so it takes in 30 CO₂ molecules.

The other numbers in the equation scale the same way. Every glucose is made with six water molecules and comes with six oxygen molecules, so five glucose molecules use 30 water molecules and release 30 oxygen molecules. Scaling up from one glucose is multiplication.
Use the same counting for a smaller batch.

Atoms are only half of the story. Joining carbon dioxide and water into glucose takes work, because the glucose holds more energy than the molecules that went into it. That energy comes from light. The chloroplasts catch some of the light that falls on the leaf and use it to build the glucose.
The energy is not lost when it is used. It is stored in the bonds that hold the glucose together, and energy stored in this way is called chemical energy.

So the atoms and the energy reach the leaf by different routes. The atoms come from carbon dioxide and water, and the energy comes from light and ends up as chemical energy in the glucose. The sugar is a store that the leaf can draw on later, even in the dark. How a cell gets the energy back out is the subject of the next lesson.
The glucose is more than a heap of atoms.

A leaf makes sugar faster in brighter light, up to a point. Measure the rate at different light levels and plot it, and the curve rises at first and then flattens, so that brighter light makes no more difference.

afterFigure.text: A flat curve means that something else is holding the rate down. Photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and water together, and it can go no faster than the scarcest of them allows. Whatever is in shortest supply is the limiting factor. In the figure the leaf with less carbon dioxide levels off sooner and lower, and the leaf with more carbon dioxide keeps climbing. For the lower curve the limit is the carbon dioxide supply and not the light. Extra light helps only while light is the thing in short supply.

lead.text: A leaf was given a fixed, low supply of CO₂. Its rate was measured at several light levels. Compare two readings to see what extra light did.

lesson.orientation: Trace carbon and energy through the overall photosynthesis reaction.
lesson.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Suppose you plant a sapling in a large tub of soil. The sapling weighs 2 kg. You dry and weigh the soil as well, and then you give the tree nothing but rainwater for years.
When it has grown the tree weighs 77 kg, which is 75 kg more than it started with. You weigh the soil again. It has lost only 60 grams.

Matter cannot appear from nothing, so the 75 kg must have come from somewhere other than the soil. This lesson follows the atoms in the tree's body back to where they came from, using the numbers and what a tree is made of as clues. It then writes down the process that built them and looks at the energy that drives it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say where a leaf's carbon comes from, count molecules with the overall equation and keep matter and energy apart.

recap.keyIdea: Photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies the energy, which the plant stores in the sugar.

blocks.text: The tree's extra 75 kg came from the air and from water, and almost none of it from the soil. You counted how many molecules of carbon dioxide, water and oxygen go with each glucose, and you kept the atoms, which come from the gases and water, apart from the energy, which comes from light. A flat curve showed that something other than light was setting the pace.

recap.nextHook: The glucose a leaf makes stores energy, and the next lesson starts with a burning candle to see how a cell gets that energy back out.

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies the carbon atoms in a leaf's newly made sugar.
hints: Rainwater has almost no carbon and light has no atoms.
Which gas carries carbon into a leaf?
It is the gas you breathe out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Light brings energy; the atoms for the sugar come from the gas.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Look for the gas that contains carbon.
Light is energy. It has no atoms to give.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in both glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms.
Each CO₂ contributes one carbon atom.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two glucose contain 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, so they need 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the carbon atoms in the sugar, because each came from one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is enough for one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, in what form is light energy stored?
hints: Think of the sugar the plant makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthesis captures some incoming light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

questions.onCorrect: Chemical energy, held in the bonds of sugar. Light itself adds no matter.

misconceptions.feedback: Some energy is lost as heat, but the energy that is captured is stored differently.
Carbon is matter. The question asks about the form of the energy.

questions.prompt: A leaf has a low supply of CO₂. Its photosynthetic rate is 8 at light level 60 and 8 at light level 80. By how much did the rate increase?
hints: Use the two rates given for the lower curve.
Subtract the first rate from the second.
What is the difference between two equal rates?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0. The curve is flat between those light levels.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The curve has plateaued, so something else, here the CO₂ supply, is limiting the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate itself, not the change in it.
That is the change in light level, not in the rate.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. Name the process, besides photosynthesis, that it uses to transfer energy from sugar.
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. Photosynthesis stores the energy, and respiration releases it for the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the process the question rules out. Name the other one.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: Read the number written in front of O₂.
Use that number of oxygen molecules for each glucose.
Multiply by three glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Six O₂ come with each glucose, so scale by the number of glucose molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are three.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the oxygen made for each one.

questions.prompt: A plant is given CO₂ whose carbon atoms are labelled. Name the kind of molecule the labelled carbon ends up in.
hints: Where does the carbon from CO₂ go?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The carbon from CO₂ is built into sugar such as glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Sugar. The carbon from CO₂ is built into glucose, so the label follows the carbon.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is released as a product, and it comes from water. The label rides on carbon.

questions.prompt: A leaf makes four glucose molecules. How many water molecules does that use, using the simplified equation?
hints: Read the number in front of H₂O.
That number is for one glucose.
Multiply by four glucose molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 24. Six water molecules go in for each glucose, so scale by the number made.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are four.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the water used for each.

questions.prompt: Where did nearly all of the tree's new mass come from?
hints: How much mass did the soil lose compared with the tree's gain?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of a tree's new mass is built from carbon dioxide in the air and from water.

questions.onCorrect: The air and water. Plants build their bodies from carbon dioxide and water, not from the soil.

misconceptions.feedback: The soil lost almost nothing, so it cannot account for such a large gain.
Light carries energy, but it adds no atoms to the tree.

questions.prompt: In the overall equation, how many CO₂ molecules go in for one glucose molecule?
hints: Read the number written in front of CO₂.
Find CO₂ on the left-hand side of the equation.
It matches the number of carbon atoms in glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equation starts 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light, so six CO₂ per glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Six. One glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ brings one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.
That is the number of hydrogen atoms in glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.

questions.prompt: Why does the number of CO₂ molecules equal the number of carbon atoms in the sugar?
hints: Count the carbon atoms inside one CO₂.

acceptedIdeas: Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each CO₂ contains one carbon atom, and every carbon atom in the sugar came from one.

choices.label: Light supplies the rest of the carbon
Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom

questions.onCorrect: Each CO₂ carries one carbon atom, so counting carbon atoms counts CO₂ molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is energy and has no atoms.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen only. The carbon comes from the gas.
